title: Parlor music, reading and learning cornet from a method book
summary: Tom explains that people wanted head music not notes, called him parlor music, and that knowing the divisions and scale let him teach himself cornet from a method book.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Well what kind of music were people playing in those days?

Well, right kind, just any little thing you hear. Yeah. Any little thing you hear, the other fellow play, you catch that. He wasn't playing no, he wasn't with the orchestration music, he wouldn't stand about that. You see? He used to call it parlor music. I used to go to play, there was a fish fry, they said don't play that, put the notes down. They didn't want the notes. You know what I'm saying? They called it parlor music in them times. They wanted the redhead music. And then the little thing you hear. You see? You sing a song, you catch that song and go play. You see? That's what we used to play. Now me, I know it was rag time, you know, I always played music. But they used to call me parlor music. And then when the time there was, the music time comes and everybody had to read, they You understand? I had to show them different things. Yeah, the division and everything like that. You see I learned that before I picked up my horn, you see. When I first started playing violin, when I learned about, I stayed about almost a month or two or three months before the division. You don't know the division, you just want to start playing music. You see, you got to know the division. Know the notes, half notes, whole notes, sixty-fold, thirty-second, you have to know all that, you understand, before. Well I know that. That's why I learned the horn. You see I didn't have to go, all I wanted to know was the scale. Well I could pick up any kind of instrument, because I know the music, just get the music and I could play, you see. I only want to know the scale. After you get the scale and the thing, well you know when you make A, you know when you make C, D, that's all you want to know. Well the music is right there, but you see that made it easy for me. Nobody didn't learn me to know a cornet. I learned it myself, you see, because I know the music. And I bought me a method, a cornet method, so I just went right on. I know the division. I played with Ullett, once or twice. You heard of anybody, Ullett? No. Old professor?
